KEY MESSAGE 1...Intermittent showers continue through Wednesday
providing some scattered help for ongoing drought conditions.

KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...
A quasi-stationary front currently extends from SW to NE across
the northern most portions of the CWA. The front as of 2AM EDT
roughly extends from Van Buren back SW to Turner Brook and near
St. Zacharie along the Quebec Maine Borderlands. Can just pick
up the boundary via satellite data using the Nighttime
Microphysics scheme. Hi-res CAMs have this boundary drifting 
southeast today slowly as it begins to washout over the CWA. At 
the same time surface low pressure deepens near Georges Bank in 
the Gulf of Maine. A very weak vort max will pass over the CWA 
during the day today. Any fog and low ceilings this morning will
break and allow for some daytime heating north of the front and
south of the front with very little sunshine near the front.
However, any sunshine near the boundary will allow for isolated
to scattered showers to develop. Enough lift from the boundary
and any daytime heating could lead to a thunderstorm but much of
any convection today will be just showers. Confidence is low-
moderate on lightning since activity will struggle to climb high
enough to develop ice aloft. Temperatures will generally be in
the 70s across the area but much more humid with dew points in
upper 60s to near 70F along and south of the front. Any showers
may produce brief heavy downpours which will be helpful to the
ongoing D0-D1 drought conditions but widespread rainfall is
unlikely. 

Another round of showers and potentially a few thunderstorms is
expected tomorrow afternoon. Todays quasi-stationary front will
wash out and tomorrow a cold front will approach from the NW
along with a 500mb shortwave. The front will be rapidly
weakening as it moves into our CWA so showers and isolated
thunderstorms will be confined to mainly northern areas. A few
degrees warmer tomorrow in the 70s to low 80s with 5-10 degree
lower dew points, except mid to upper 60s along the Downeast
coast. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Areas of fog early this AM then again tonight. 
Fog could be patchy dense at times and impact travel. Dense fog 
is most likely in places that receive showers during the day. 

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...
Patchy to areas of fog this morning across areas along and south
of the quasi-stationary front in the more moist/humid airmass.
Any showers today will be the focus for more fog tonight given
the light and variable winds expected. Patchy to areas of dense
fog is possible but confidence is low on how widespread the fog
will be based on the scattered nature of showers during the day.
Nighttime dense fog always adds challenges to driving conditions
with significant wildlife activity at night. 

KEY MESSAGE 3... There is the potential for widespread rainfall
from Sunday into Monday. It is not certain how much, if any, 
relief this could bring to the developing drought at this time.

KEY MESSAGE 3 DESCRIPTION...
A closed low tracks from near the Great Lakes on Sunday to
southwestern Quebec/Northern New England by Monday evening. 
There is always more uncertainty than normal when talking about 
closed lows, as models in general do not have a good track 
record on the timing or track of these systems. With that said, 
it is shown in some form in more ensembles than not, with 
similar timing, so that does somewhat mitigate the typical 
uncertainty for these types of systems. 

Based on the ensemble consensus would expect warm advection
rain, with embedded convection from Sunday through Monday. The 
latter is most likely in the afternoon/early evening. At this 
point in time, given the inherent uncertainty in days 6 and 7 in
the forecast, plus the added uncertainty given the storm type 
(even if somewhat mitigated by a degree of consensus in the 
ensembles), it is to early to state what, if any, impacts this 
system may have on the region.
